v.q: What does an API gateway typically do?
o: One entry point that routes calls and handles auth and rate limits
A central store holding the data for every service
A replacement for service discovery inside the cluster
A place that runs the business logic of every service
v.w: It hides the internal topology from clients. Keep business logic out of it to avoid a distributed monolith.

v.q: Which job should an API gateway NOT take on?
o: Storing service data
Routing requests
Authenticating callers
Rate limiting
v.w: A gateway is an entry point. Data belongs to the services that own it.

v.q: A downstream service is failing and slow. What does a circuit breaker do?
o: Stops calling for a while and fails fast, then probes for recovery
Retries as fast as possible until a response arrives
Restarts the failing downstream service itself
Caches every response for ever after
v.w: States are closed, open and half-open. Failing fast frees threads and gives the failing service room to recover.

v.q: Which state of a circuit breaker lets a few trial calls through?
o: Half-open
Open
Closed
Tripped
v.w: After the wait time the breaker tries a few calls. If they succeed it closes, otherwise it opens again.

v.q: Why is retrying a failed call with no delay dangerous?
o: It can overload a struggling service; use backoff with jitter
Retries are not allowed over HTTP at all
Retries always create duplicate data
Retries automatically disable the circuit breaker
v.w: Synchronised retries create a retry storm. Backoff spreads load and jitter stops clients from retrying in lockstep. Retry only idempotent calls.

v.q: Which retry policy is NOT safe for an overloaded service?
o: Retry at once with no delay
Exponential backoff
Backoff with jitter
A limit on retry attempts
v.w: Immediate retries multiply the load on a service that is already struggling.

v.q: What does the bulkhead pattern protect against?
o: One slow dependency using all threads and sinking the service
Data being lost after a disk failure
Unauthorised users reaching internal services
Version mismatches between two deployed services
v.w: Isolating resources (separate pools per dependency) contains the failure, like watertight compartments in a ship.

v.q: A slow reporting API uses all threads of a shared pool, and payments stop. Which pattern prevents it?
o: Bulkhead
Strangler fig
Saga
Adapter
v.w: Separate pools keep one slow dependency from starving the others.

v.q: Which statement about the database-per-service pattern is correct?
o: Each service owns its data; others use its API or events
All services share one schema for easy joins
Services read each other's tables directly for speed
Only a single service is allowed a database
v.w: It enables independent deployment and scaling, but cross-service queries and consistency need new patterns such as sagas and CQRS views.

o: Joining another service tables directly
Calling the owner API
Subscribing to the owner events
Keeping a local copy built from events
v.w: Reading another service tables couples the two and removes its freedom to change its schema.

o: Services find the current network locations of other services
Services are scanned automatically for security flaws
Request latency is measured for every call
Service traffic is encrypted in transit
v.w: Instances come and go. A registry (Eureka, Consul) or the platform DNS (Kubernetes services) keeps track of healthy instances.

v.q: What does a service registry such as Eureka, or Kubernetes DNS, provide?
o: Instance addresses
Business data
User passwords
Compiled code
v.w: Instances come and go, so callers look up where a service is running now.

v.q: What is the strangler fig pattern used for?
o: Gradually replace a legacy system by routing slices to new services
Kill any request that takes too long to be answered
Compress the responses coming from the older services
Rewrite everything and release it in a single big bang
v.w: A facade routes some traffic to the new code while the rest still hits the old system, until the old one can be switched off.

v.q: Which statement about the strangler fig pattern is NOT true?
o: It needs a single big-bang release
It migrates slice by slice
It routes some calls to new services
The old system shrinks over time
v.w: The strangler approach avoids big-bang releases by replacing pieces gradually.

o: The model that writes (commands) from the model that reads (queries)
The front end of an app from its back end
Test code from the production code that it checks
Public APIs from the private APIs of a service
v.w: Read models can be denormalised and scaled on their own, updated from events. It adds eventual consistency, so use it where reads and writes differ a lot.

v.q: Which statement about CQRS is NOT true?
o: Reads and writes must use the same model
It separates commands from queries
The read side can use its own store
It can add eventual consistency
v.w: CQRS exists to let the two sides use different models.
